items.title: PLFR 2026 : quand le Parlement tape du poing sur la table pour exiger un électrochoc budgétaire
items.description: A quelques heures seulement de l'adoption décisive du volet recettes du Projet de Loi de Finances Rectificative (PLFR) 2026, l’Assemblée nationale a jeté un pavé dans la mare. Au terme de semaines de concertations serrées avec les départements ministériels, la Banque Centrale et les grandes institutions de la République, les députés ont accouché d'un rapport de synthèse sans concession, assorti de 23 recommandations musclées. Si les élus de la nation saluent unanimement les embellies macroéconomiques de ces derniers mois marquées notamment par le passage de la Guinée de la catégorie 7 à la catégorie 6 à l'OCDE et l'obtention de la convoitée notation souveraine B+, le message adressé à l'exécutif ne laisse place à aucune ambiguïté : la croissance et les bons indicateurs ne valent que s'ils profitent directement aux citoyens et se traduisent par une souveraineté financière intraitable. Le secteur minier et les niches fiscales dans le collimateur C'est incontestablement le dossier le plus brûlant de cette session budgétaire. Les parlementaires se sont penchés avec une minutie chirurgicale sur les exonérations et régimes dérogatoires dont bénéficie le secteur extractif. Les chiffres révélés ont de quoi donner le vertige : en 2025, le coût budgétaire des seules dépenses fiscales douanières s'est élevé à 11 793 milliards GNF — soit près de 48 % des recettes douanières collectées, l'équivalent de la construction d'au moins 100 kilomètres de routes bitumées. En y ajoutant l'ardoise de la Direction Générale des Impôts (DGI) pour les neuf premiers mois de 2026, c'est un pactole de plus de 15 666 milliards GNF auquel l'État a renoncé pour des motifs sociaux ou économiques. Plus troublant encore aux yeux de la représentation nationale : sur 128 mesures recensées en 2023, à peine 10 dispositions dérogatoires (soit moins de 8 %) concentrent à elles seules 67 % des pertes définitives de l'État. Face à cette hémorragie, le Parlement exige du Gouvernement une révision sans délai de l'article 18 du Code minier et de l'article 33 du Code des investissements. Autre motif d'incompréhension soulevé par les commissions : l'absence criante d'équipements de mesure modernes. « Il est inadmissible qu'un pays comme la Guinée, premier producteur de fer et deuxième de bauxite au monde, ne dispose pas de ponts-bascules et de laboratoires de référence pour certifier avec exactitude le volume et la qualité des minerais qu'il exporte », s'indigne un proche des travaux parlementaires. Or artisanal : la fin de l'exception au rabais Dans l'hémicycle, la question de l'or artisanal a également fait l'objet d'un réquisitoire particulièrement documenté. Alors que ce secteur pèse près de 70 % des exportations aurifères du pays, il demeurait jusqu'ici taxé au poids de manière forfaitaire, à hauteur de 50 dollars américains par kilogramme — soit un taux dérisoire de 0,06 % de sa valeur réelle. À titre de comparaison, l'or industriel s'acquitte de 5 % de sa valeur (environ 6 535 USD/kg), tandis que les pays voisins de la sous-région, comme le Mali ou le Burkina Faso, appliquent des taux oscillant entre 3 % et 4 %. En Guinée, un kilogramme d'or artisanal rapportait à peine 460 000 GNF au Trésor public, contre plus de 22 millions de francs guinéens chez ses voisins maliens. En réponse, les députés ont sifflé la fin de la récréation en exigeant l'application stricte et immédiate de l'article 164 du Code minier. Le prélèvement passera ainsi à 1 % de la valeur, faisant grimper la contribution de 50 à environ 1 307 USD par kilo, un compromis jugé idéal pour doper les réserves en devises de la Banque centrale et stabiliser le franc guinéen, tout en restant suffisamment compétitif pour dissuader les contrebandiers. Entre dérapages institutionnels et rappels à l'ordre Le rapport de l'Assemblée nationale ne s'arrête pas aux frontières des mines et égrène une série de dysfonctionnements administratifs et institutionnels qui ont mis le feu aux poudres lors des débats. L'un des épisodes les plus marquants demeure l'affaire de l'Autorité de Régulation des Jeux et Pratiques Assimilées (ARSJPA). En février 2025, cette structure s'était illustrée en instruisant par courrier aux opérateurs de refuser d'acquitter les taxes légalement votées par le Parlement (15 % sur le produit brut des jeux et 7 % de prélèvement BNC sur les gains). Un camouflet institutionnel qualifié par les députés de violation flagrante de la hiérarchie des normes, assorti d'une exigence de mise en conformité de son statut d'autorité indépendante. Dans la même veine, les élus ont pointé la lenteur exaspérante du recouvrement des créances fiscales. Sur 1 532 milliards GNF de créances identifiées auprès de 45 grandes entreprises dans le cadre d'un audit appuyé par la BAD, seuls 208 milliards GNF ont été encaissés à ce jour. Pour récupérer les 992 milliards restants, le Parlement suggère de passer à la vitesse supérieure en sollicitant l'appui du Haut Commandement de la Gendarmerie nationale. Quant au volet des assurances, l'application stricte du décret sur l'obligation de couvrir les importations auprès des compagnies locales agréées pourrait injecter près de 300 millions de dollars de primes par an dans l'économie nationale, au lieu de voir ces capitaux s'envoler systématiquement à l'étranger. Tourner la page de l'attentisme Qu'il s'agisse de l'apurement des 550 milliards GNF de crédits de TVA en souffrance pour préserver la trésorerie des entreprises, de la transparence exigée autour des fonds du Service Universel (FSU), ou encore de la traçabilité des avoirs saisis et confisqués par la justice — dont le Trésor public n'a pas encore vu la couleur —, ce PLFR 2026 fait office d'électrochoc. En clôturant ces travaux marathon, la représentation nationale a tenu à rappeler une vérité première à l'exécutif : les notations financières flatteuses et les classements internationaux n'ont de sens que s'ils guérissent les maux du quotidien. Assainissement de la circulation fiduciaire pour en finir avec les billets usés, accélération des décaissement de projets extérieurs pour éviter les pénalités d'engagement, et rigueur implacable dans la collecte des ressources domestiques : Conakry retient son souffle, attendant de voir ces résolutions se matérialiser sur le terrain.

items.title: MIIF leads 50-hectare forest restoration project in Sekyere Krobo
items.description: The Minerals Income Investment Fund (MIIF), in partnership with the Forestry Commission and supported by Zijin Golden Ridge Ghana and other partners has commissioned a five-year project to restore 50 hectares of degraded forest at the Subri River Forest Reserve in Sekyere Krobo, Western Region. The project, commissioned on October 29, 2026, forms part of MIIF’s Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) Biodiversity Reforestation Project, which seeks to promote environmental sustainability and strengthen biodiversity conservation in Ghana’s mining regions. Protecting Ghana’s natural heritage Speaking at the commissioning ceremony, MIIF Chief Executive Officer, Justina Nelson, said the initiative reflects the Fund’s commitment to ensuring that the economic benefits of mineral resources are matched by responsible environmental stewardship. “The true value of our nation’s mineral wealth lies not only in what we extract today, but also in the natural heritage we preserve for generations to come,” she said. She emphasised that the success of the project would not be measured simply by the number of trees planted, but by the extent to which the forest is restored and protected over time. This, she noted, would require sustained care, effective monitoring and the collective commitment of all stakeholders. The Forestry Commission is providing technical expertise and implementation support to guide the rehabilitation process and promote the long-term survival of the restored forest. The Executive Director of the Forest Services Division of the Forestry Commission, Dr Sarfo Adu, highlighted the importance of sustained collaboration and effective forest management in achieving successful restoration. He said the Commission would provide technical guidance and implementation support to ensure the restoration work was effectively managed and that the trees planted survived to support the forest’s long-term recovery. He also urged other corporate organisations to draw inspiration from MIIF’s initiative and partner with the Forestry Commission to help restore Ghana’s degraded forest landscape. He said such partnerships would support the government’s Tree for Life Restoration Initiative, launched by President John Dramani Mahama on 21 March 2025. Community participation key to sustainability The Paramount Chief of Sekyere Krobo, Nana Kwao Badu II, commended MIIF and its partners for the initiative and welcomed the participation of farmers in the restoration exercise. He called on the Forestry Commission to work closely with the farmers to ensure that they also benefit from their efforts to nurture and protect the trees. He noted that recognising the role and livelihoods of local communities would encourage a stronger sense of ownership and responsibility for the forest. Nana Kwao Badu II also expressed appreciation to MIIF for providing farm tools to support participating farmers and appealed for additional support for forest guards to strengthen the protection of the reserve. His remarks highlighted the importance of combining environmental restoration with community livelihoods and effective forest protection. A collective commitment to environmental sustainability The five-year initiative brings together MIIF, the Forestry Commission and Corporate Ghana in a shared effort to address forest degradation, protect biodiversity and promote sustainable environmental practices. MIIF acknowledged the support of the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, the Forestry Commission, Corporate Ghana, traditional authorities, the District Assembly and the people of Sekyere Krobo. Through the restoration of 50 hectares of degraded forest, the Fund is reinforcing its commitment to responsible mineral wealth management and ensuring that environmental protection remains an important part of Ghana’s sustainable development agenda.

items.title: JOJ Dakar 2026 : un spectacle grandiose pour une première africaine
items.description: Le Sénégal a ouvert, samedi soir, une nouvelle page de l’histoire olympique africaine avec la cérémonie d’ouverture des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026, au stade Abdoulaye-Wade de Diamniadio. En présence du président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, de plusieurs dirigeants étrangers et de personnalités du mouvement olympique, le spectacle a célébré l’identité sénégalaise et la diversité culturelle africaine à travers des tableaux artistiques, des chorégraphies et des prestations musicales. Cette cérémonie marque une première historique : l’organisation des JOJ sur le continent africain. Elle ouvre deux semaines de compétitions réunissant quelque 2 700 athlètes autour de 25 disciplines sportives. Au-delà de la compétition, Dakar 2026 offre au Sénégal et à l’Afrique une vitrine internationale pour mettre en valeur leur patrimoine culturel, leur hospitalité et leur ambition sportive. Salla GUEYE

items.title: GAYO partners with MMDAs and schools to promote waste segregation in Greater Accra
items.description: The Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) has partnered with metropolitan, municipal, and district assemblies and schools across Greater Accra to promote waste segregation among students. The initiative, under GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, covers schools in seven municipalities, including La Dade Kotopon, Ledzokuku, Accra Metropolitan and Ablekuma West. It aims to help schools separate their waste at source, turn organic waste into compost, and recycle plastics. Betty Adjei, Operations and Programs Director at GAYO, said the initiative comes ahead of a government directive requiring all households to start separating their waste from next year. “When is the important time to support with infrastructure, to support this kind of policy?” she said. “It’s very important to catch them young.” As part of the initiative, GAYO is distributing 200 bins, 300 books, pens and educational flyers to schools across the seven municipalities. Each school receives two bins to help students separate their waste. Ms Adjei said the initiative will later extend to markets and wider municipalities. Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi, a Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, said about 60 percent of the financial resources given to assemblies go into managing waste. A waste analysis by GAYO found that about 60 percent of the waste generated in schools is organic. “And so we are helping these schools to be able to separate their waste,” he said. “The organic waste is turned into what is called compost.” He said the compost is used in school gardens to grow vegetables free of the chemicals found in synthetic fertilisers. GAYO is also training students to make compost themselves, while plastics will go to its material recovery facility to be processed into pellets. The partnership also tackles a problem that has frustrated schools. Madam Habiba Kotomah, Education Director for the La Dade Kotopon Municipality, said schools that sorted their waste in the past saw it mixed back together by collection trucks. She welcomed GAYO’s plan to collect the separated waste directly and pay schools a token in return. “So they will come around and pick the organic ones and pick the plastic ones,” she said. “I’m so happy my schools are going to be able to generate some form of IGF from this activity.” Ms Adjei said the approach builds on work already underway. The La Dade Kotopon Municipal Assembly’s material recovery facility diverts more than 50 tonnes of waste a month. At Forces Senior High School, Assistant Headmistress (Domestic) Rosina Lawal said the school has already placed bins within reach of students, and wants more. “Imagine we have bins like one student, one bin. The school, and not only the school, the whole of Ghana will also look very beautiful,” she said. She urged GAYO to keep going: “They should add more, like Oliver Twist, we want more.” Reducing organic waste in landfills also helps cut methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. More than half of the waste Accra produces is organic. In October 2026, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly warned that Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030.

items.title: GAYO, some Accra schools turn to composting and recycling to beat the waste problem with fresh bins
items.description: Schools in Accra that separate their waste say their efforts are being wasted because collection trucks mix the sorted rubbish back together when they pick it up. Education officials in the La Dade Kotopon Municipality say the problem has led many schools to give up sorting altogether. Now, the Green Africa Youth Organization (GAYO) wants to change that. Under its Zero Waste initiative, it plans to collect separated organic and plastic waste directly from schools in seven municipalities across Greater Accra. Madam Habiba Kotomah, Education Director for the La Dade Kotopon Municipality, said some schools were part of an earlier pilot that provided bins for sorting, but the effort collapsed at the point of collection. “We do the sorting in the schools. But when the truck comes around, they put everything back together and it’s frustrating,” she said. “So at a point, most of them stopped the sorting.” She said schools also lack enough bins, despite repeated requests to the assembly. Waste is a heavy burden on local government. Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi, a Project Coordinator on GAYO’s Zero Waste portfolio, said about 60 percent of the financial resources given to assemblies go into managing waste, mostly organic waste and plastics. Schools are a major source. “Per the waste analysis that we’ve done, we found out that about 60 percent of the waste that is generated in the school is organic waste, followed by papers and then plastics,” he said. When organic waste is dumped and left to rot, it produces methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide. More than half of all the waste Accra produces is organic, and most of it ends up in landfills. In October 2026, officials of the Accra Metropolitan Assembly warned that Ghana risks missing its target of cutting methane emissions from the waste sector by 30 percent by 2030. Poorly managed waste also has more visible costs. Betty Adjei, Operations and Programs Director at GAYO, pointed to the floods in June and July. “We saw what happened during the June-July flooding, where a lot of waste were within our communities,” she said. She said the push for schools comes ahead of a government directive requiring all households to start separating their waste from next year. “It’s very important to catch them young,” she said. Under the initiative, GAYO is working with schools in the La Dade Kotopon, Ledzokuku, Accra Metropolitan and Ablekuma West municipalities, among others, to set up sorting systems and train students. Separated organic waste is turned into compost for school gardens. Mr Antonio Yayrator Korkuvi said vegetables grown with the compost are free of the chemicals found in synthetic fertilisers. Plastics will go to GAYO’s material recovery facility to be processed into pellets. Madam Kotomah said GAYO has agreed to collect the sorted waste from schools and pay them a token in return. “So they will come around and pick the organic ones and pick the plastic ones,” she said. “I’m so happy my schools are going to be able to generate some form of IGF from this activity.” Ms Adjei said the model is already working at municipal level. The La Dade Kotopon Municipal Assembly’s material recovery facility diverts more than 50 tonnes of waste a month, from organics to plastics. She said the initiative will later extend to markets. At Forces Senior High School, Assistant Headmistress (Domestic) Rosina Lawal has built a culture of keeping bins within reach of every student. She said her goal is one bin for every student. “Imagine we have bins like one student, one bin. The school, and even not only the school, the whole Ghana will look very beautiful,” she said. She admitted that enforcing cleanliness has not made her popular. “Parents may talk, the students may hate you, but the fact is, me, I want to make a name,” she said. “You could see the whole school is looking nice.” She urged GAYO and other partners to keep going. “They should add more, like Oliver Twist, we want more,” she said. “They shouldn’t relax.”

items.title: Why Financing Government is more rewarding in Africa than financing enterprise and the threat to economic integration
items.description: The gradual implementation of the African Continental Free Trade Area has brought greater focus on the advantages of significantly increasing intra-African trade from the current 16%–17%. It is recognised that Africa’s economic integration will make it more rewarding to produce, invest and trade, boosting growth, jobs and shared prosperity across Africa and her 1.5 billion-strong population. The campaign now, and rightly so, is about getting African governments to enable two low-hanging key drivers of intra-African trade: visa-free travel and connected payment systems that allow Africans to move freely, buy and sell across borders using simply their mobile money wallets. This is because, according to the research desk of the Africa Prosperity Network (APN), these two moves alone can increase intra-African trade to more than 25% within the first five years of implementation. Once a tailor or seamstress in Bamako can promote his or her clothes on Instagram, a customer in Maputo can buy instantly online using her mobile money wallet in Mozambican meticais, her local currency, and the seller can receive payment right then in West African CFA francs, opening that commercial highway will create the incentive for investors and financiers to put money into the transport and logistics that will ensure that goods sold across borders in Africa get to buyers in no time. It is through this lens that I welcome the statement from Ghana’s President, John Dramani Mahama, in Moscow on 29 October 2026. His call for local-currency trade settlements and integrated digital payments, alongside greater local processing of Africa’s mineral and agricultural resources, brings together two priorities too often discussed separately: producing more value in Africa and making it easier to trade that value across Africa. But, fundamentally, Africa’s single market must make it more rewarding to produce, invest and trade. Removing visa restrictions and connecting payment systems are essential: Africans should be able to travel across the continent and buy and sell across borders using their mobile money wallets. But easier movement and payments will achieve far more if the businesses expected to serve that market can also access affordable finance. This brings us to a damaging incentive in many African economies, which is that financing government can be more rewarding than financing enterprise. When governments borrow heavily at high interest rates, banks and investors can earn attractive returns from Treasury bills and bonds, with fewer operational demands than investing in production, the real economy. Manufacturers need machinery, reliable electricity and skilled workers; agribusinesses face weather risks and seasonal cash flows. These enterprises create jobs, yet they struggle to attract capital or even borrow from the banks when government securities offer compelling returns. High nominal yields do not necessarily mean high real returns: inflation and currency depreciation can erode them. Government bonds can also finance infrastructure that enables enterprise. The problem arises when persistent deficits absorb scarce savings and push up borrowing costs for businesses. America offers a warning from a different stage of development. Its relative decline in manufacturing dominance, particularly against China, is often attributed partly to financialization, which is the growing influence of financial returns and shareholder valuations over business decisions. Critics argue that maximising share prices and short-term payouts can take precedence over expanding productive capacity. In Africa, the danger is that financing government becomes more rewarding than financing enterprise. In America, it is that maximising financial valuations becomes more important than expanding productive capacity. The mechanisms differ, but the common danger is finance becoming detached from the production that sustains prosperity. America built a formidable industrial base before these concerns emerged. Africa, however, has yet to industrialise at the scale our population demands. We cannot afford to starve production of capital before building that foundation. This is why affordable finance belongs at the heart of Africa’s integration agenda. A functioning single market serving some 1.5 billion people would strengthen the commercial case for factories, agricultural processing and regional supply chains. But market access alone cannot finance machinery or fulfil an order. Without stronger African production, we risk integrating markets largely for goods made elsewhere. This is also why we at the Africa Prosperity Network welcome the Africa Credit Rating Agency. Its inaugural CEO, Dr Sifiso Falala, brings experience from challenging established rating practices through his work at Plus 94. AfCRA will help institutionalise and tackle the issue of how African risks are assessed and, ultimately, how productive investment can secure affordable finance. Integration and sound economic management must therefore advance together. Low, stable inflation makes long-term investment easier to plan. Credible public finances and sustainable government borrowing reduce competition for scarce savings. Reliable electricity, predictable taxation and enforceable contracts improve the prospects of productive enterprise. Simply ordering interest rates down cannot substitute for these foundations. The objective for our continent is a connected economic system: a larger market makes investment more attractive; affordable, patient capital makes production possible; and efficient transport and payments help businesses reach customers and get paid. Our focus now at APN, with the support of our partners, is to go for these two quick wins of cross-border digital payments interoperability and visa-free travel. Local processing requires investment. Investment needs viable markets. Those markets need practical ways to move people, goods and money. President Mahama’s call at the Russia-Africa Summit thus speaks directly to the challenge of making African enterprise more competitive and rewarding. Its promise will be fully realised when national economic policies support the producers whom continental integration is intended to empower. His reaffirmation of Nkrumah’s vision of African unity is encouraging. His anticipated African Union chairmanship in 2027, coinciding with Ghana’s 70th independence anniversary, would offer an opportunity to rally fellow leaders behind this practical economic Pan-Africanism. Africa Prosperity Dialogues 2027 provides a timely platform to translate that ambition into proposals for action. Its theme, “The Borderless Africa We Want: Move Freely. Pay Seamlessly. Trade More,” captures the connections between mobility, payments and commerce. The financing argument gives that agenda its productive foundation, which is that African businesses must be able to make what this larger market needs. Hosted by President Mahama in Ghana on 13–15 January 2027, with strategic partners including AfDB, Afreximbank, BADEA, AUDA-NEPAD and major African multinational companies, the Dialogues, fifth in the annual series, will bring private sector and civil society perspectives into the deliberations preceding the 40th AU Summit. More so because its focus connects directly with the AU’s 2027 theme, “AU at the Dawn of its 25th Anniversary: Leveraging the Full Potential of SAATM and New Technologies for Continental Integration.” The Single African Air Transport Market and new technologies can help connect businesses and consumers across our fragmented continent. Alongside freer movement and interoperable payments, they can make the single market more accessible to those expected to build it. APD 2027 must help turn these connections into a coherent agenda for our leaders: remove barriers to trade while improving the conditions for production. The experiences of those who invest, employ and trade should inform the policies intended to serve them. The measure of success will be more African savings financing African enterprises, more resources processed locally and more young people finding worthwhile work. Our single market will, thus, fulfil its promise when it makes it pay to produce right here in Africa. The author is the Founder and Executive Chairman of the Africa Prosperity Network, organisers of Africa Prosperity Dialogues 2027. To register, visit www.apd2027.africaprosperitynetwork.com or email gabby@africaprosperity.network.

items.title: Video captures teachers stepping on a student’s head in violent Techiman SHS incident
items.description: A disturbing video circulating on social media has revealed a violent incident at Techiman Senior High School (SHS) in the Bono East Region, showing two teachers assaulting a final-year student. The video footage, which has sparked outrage, shows the two men assaulting the student, including stepping on the student’s head. The teachers involved have been identified as Mr Jerry Jones Owusu Bekoe and Mr Adusa Ameyaw. The incident has been referred to the Ghana Education Service (GES) for urgent investigation following instructions from the Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu. Deputy Minister for Education, Dr Clement Abas Apaak, confirmed the directive in a Facebook post. “At the instance of the Honourable Minister for Education, Haruna Iddrisu, I have referred the attached disturbing video—said to be a violent incident at Techiman SHS involving some teachers and a student—to the Director-General of the Ghana Education Service for urgent investigation,” Dr Apaak stated. He added that the Director-General has been directed to apply the necessary sanctions to the offending parties. “Misconduct will not be tolerated in our schools from any stakeholder, be it teaching and non-teaching staff, students or parents. We have a mandate to ensure that our schools remain safe for all—students, teaching and non-teaching staff—at all times,” he stated. The GES, in a statement issued on October 31, 2026 and signed by Head of Public Relations Daniel Fenyi, said the school’s disciplinary committee held its initial hearing on the matter. “The committee’s findings are expected to be submitted to Management through the Regional Directorate in the coming days to inform further action and decisions,” the statement read. The affected student has been identified as Seedorf Abeka Ampah, a final-year Agricultural Science student. The GES said he has received medical attention and is responding positively to treatment. The GES has urged the public to remain calm as it conducts thorough investigations into the matter.

items.title: Tour du Faso 2026 : La BCB réaffirme son engagement aux côtés du cyclisme burkinabè
items.description: La Banque Commerciale du Burkina (BCB) renouvelle son engagement en faveur du sport national, particulièrement du cyclisme. Présente au lancement de la 37e édition du Tour du Faso, le vendredi 30 octobre 2026, l’institution bancaire entend, à travers cet accompagnement, soutenir la jeunesse burkinabè et rester proche des populations et confirmer son rôle de banque du tour. La Banque commerciale du Burkina (BCB) confirme son engagement aux côtés du sport burkinabè. À l’occasion de la 37e édition du Tour du Faso, la banque nationale a réaffirmé son soutien à cette compétition cycliste majeure. Pour Safiatou Kiemtoré/Sana, chef service animation commerciale de la BCB, cet accompagnement traduit la volonté de l’institution de contribuer à l’épanouissement de la jeunesse. « La Banque commerciale du Burkina ne cesse d’accompagner la jeunesse burkinabè et qui parle de jeunesse parle de sport », a-t-elle déclaré. Au-delà du soutien à la compétition, la BCB entend également renforcer ses liens avec les populations et sa clientèle. « Nous accompagnons le Tour du Faso, non seulement pour être aux côtés des populations qui sont nos clients, mais aussi pour être toujours aux côtés de la jeunesse, qui est le futur du Burkina », a expliqué Safiatou Kiemtoré/Sana. « La Banque commerciale du Burkina œuvre pour l’équilibre social », Safiatou Kiemtoré/Sana Cette implication s’inscrit également dans la mission que s’est assignée la banque depuis sa nationalisation en 2024. Selon sa représentante, la BCB œuvre aussi bien pour l’équilibre social que pour le développement économique du pays, en tenant compte des différents acteurs qui contribuent à son économie. « La Banque commerciale du Burkina œuvre pour l’équilibre social, sans oublier l’économie du pays et tous les acteurs qui interviennent dans cette économie », a-t-elle souligné. La participation de la BCB à cette 37e édition se traduit également par une présence à différentes étapes de la compétition. La troisième étape, quant à elle, est spécialement dédiée à la Banque commerciale du Burkina. À travers cet accompagnement, la BCB entend inscrire son soutien au Tour du Faso dans la durée. Faso7 L’article Tour du Faso 2026 : La BCB réaffirme son engagement aux côtés du cyclisme burkinabè est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Joj Dakar 2026 : Diagna Ndiaye veut faire du Sénégal une référence olympique
items.description: Le président du Comité national olympique et sportif sénégalais (CNOSS), Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye, a appelé, samedi, à faire des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse (JOJ) Dakar 2026 un héritage durable pour l’Afrique et les générations futures, affirmant que le continent est désormais au cœur de l’histoire olympique. « Ce soir, l’Afrique n’est plus en marge des Jeux, elle en devient le cœur », a déclaré Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye lors de la cérémonie officielle d’ouverture des JOJ Dakar 2026. « Pour la première fois de l’histoire, la flamme olympique brûle sur notre continent. Pour la première fois, la jeunesse du monde est hôte de l’Afrique », a-t-il souligné, souhaitant la bienvenue aux athlètes et aux délégations venus du monde entier. Le président du CNOSS est revenu sur le processus ayant conduit à l’organisation de ces Jeux, depuis le choix de la candidature de Dakar à Buenos Aires, en 2018, jusqu’aux difficultés engendrées par la pandémie de Covid-19. Il a salué la continuité de l’État, l’engagement du comité d’organisation et l’implication des autorités sénégalaises, notamment celle du président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, dans les derniers mois de préparation. Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye a également rendu hommage aux femmes sénégalaises, représentées par les « 100 linguères des temps modernes » qui ont porté la flamme olympique à la place du Souvenir africain. « Vous avez porté la mémoire de nos mères, la force de nos communautés et la promesse de nos filles. L’Afrique avance avec ses femmes. Ce soir, le monde le voit », a-t-il déclaré. La flamme olympique, a-t-il rappelé, a parcouru les quatorze régions du Sénégal, rassemblant, autour de ce symbole, des champions et des anonymes, des jeunes et des personnes âgées. Le président du CNOSS a, par ailleurs, salué la présidente du Comité international olympique (CIO), Kirsty Coventry, première femme et première Africaine à diriger cette institution, estimant que la tenue de ses premiers Jeux à Dakar revêt une portée symbolique particulière pour le continent. S’adressant aux jeunes athlètes, il les a invités à faire des quinze jours de compétition un moment de fraternité, de respect et de rapprochement entre les peuples. « Gagnez, perdez, recommencez, mais surtout osez, osez l’amitié », leur a-t-il lancé, estimant que le plus beau record de ces Jeux ne se mesurera ni en secondes ni en médailles, mais à l’aune de « l’unité » qu’ils auront contribué à faire naître. Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye a également mis en avant les valeurs culturelles sénégalaises que sont le « Jom », associé à la dignité, le « Kersa », symbole de respect, et le « Ngor », qui renvoie au dépassement de soi. Il a insisté sur la nécessité de faire des infrastructures mobilisées pour les JOJ un patrimoine utile aux populations, notamment aux élèves, aux étudiants et aux habitants des quartiers, après la fin des compétitions. « Nous avons voulu des Jeux utiles, sobres et durables. Nous ne voulons pas laisser une charge, nous voulons laisser un héritage », a-t-il affirmé. Pour le président du CNOSS, Dakar 2026 doit ainsi porter un message d’espoir à l’Afrique et à la jeunesse mondiale, appelée à prendre en main son avenir. « Ce soir, nous n’allumons pas une flamme pour éclairer un stade, nous l’allumons pour éclairer une génération », a-t-il déclaré, invitant les jeunes à préserver cet esprit olympique et à le faire rayonner dans leurs pays respectifs. Réaffirmant l’engagement du Sénégal à organiser des Jeux sûrs, joyeux et inoubliables, Mamadou Diagna Ndiaye a exprimé son ambition de voir Dakar 2026 devenir une référence dans l’histoire olympique. « Nous ne voulons pas être une parenthèse, nous voulons être une référence », a-t-il conclu, avant de lancer : « Vive la jeunesse, vive le Sénégal, vive l’Afrique, vive l’Olympisme ! » S.G

items.title: Veto russe : Joe Wilson réclame des sanctions contre l’Algérie
items.description: Le congressman républicain dénonce la volonté de Moscou de déstabiliser l’Afrique après le blocage du projet de résolution sur le Sahara. Il exige que le polisario soit classé organisation terroriste étrangère et que le régime algérien soit frappé de sanctions CAATSA. Au lendemain du veto russe au Conseil de sécurité, le congressman américain Joe Wilson monte au créneau. Ce samedi 31 octobre, l’élu de Caroline du Sud, membre de la commission des Affaires étrangères de la Chambre des représentants, a réagi sur X en désignant sans détour les bénéficiaires du blocage : Moscou, le régime algérien, Téhéran et le polisario. Le vote s’est tenu vendredi 30 octobre. Le projet de résolution américain a recueilli onze voix pour, une contre et trois abstentions, avant de se heurter au veto de la Russie, membre permanent du Conseil. C’est la première fois que Moscou recourt à cet instrument sur ce dossier, alors qu’il s’était contenté de s’abstenir lors de l’adoption de la résolution 2797, l’an dernier. L’échéance était pressante : le mandat de la Minurso expirait le 31 octobre, et le texte rejeté prévoyait la transformation de la mission en une nouvelle entité, la Minuso, à compter du 1er novembre. Joe Wilson affirme que la résolution était largement soutenue et pleine de bon sens. elle maintenait une présence onusienne et allait dans le sens du règlement définitif du différend sur la base du plan d’autonomie soumis par le Maroc. Or, écrit-il, l’objectif de la Russie est d’aggraver la déstabilisation de l’Afrique. Le congressman nomme ensuite ceux qui tirent profit de l’impasse : la Russie, le régime algérien, qu’il range parmi ses marionnettes, l’Iran, et le polisario, adossé à Alger et entraîné par le Hezbollah. Il avait développé ce constat dès septembre 2025, en s’appuyant sur une enquête du Washington Post qui documentait la formation de combattants du polisario par le Hezbollah et la présence de drones iraniens dans son arsenal. Deux exigences suivent. La première est connue : il est « grand temps » de classer le polisario comme organisation terroriste étrangère. Ce mouvement, qui prétend parler au nom des Sahraouis, est selon Joe Wilson une milice soutenue par le régime algérien, qui agit au service des intérêts de Moscou et de Téhéran dans la région. Cette exigence s’appuie sur un texte que le congressman porte depuis plus d’un an. Il avait annoncé en avril 2025 son intention de saisir le Congrès, avant de déposer en juin 2025 à la Chambre des représentants un projet de loi visant à sanctionner le polisario et à le désigner organisation terroriste étrangère. Coparrainé par le démocrate Jimmy Panetta, ce qui lui confère un caractère bipartisan, le texte a depuis été rejoint par plusieurs élus, dont Randy Fine, Lance Gooden, Pat Harrigan et Zachary Nunn. La seconde exigence marque un net durcissement envers Alger : l’application de sanctions au titre de la CAATSA, loi américaine de 2017 qui permet de frapper les pays procédant à des achats d’armement significatifs auprès de la Russie. Joe Wilson reproche au régime algérien de constituer un arsenal d’armes russes pour semer le « chaos » en Afrique du Nord comme en Europe. Il ajoute que l’Algérie s’en sortirait bien mieux si ses dirigeants misaient sur un avenir radieux plutôt que sur le terrorisme. Cette sortie prolonge une ligne que Joe Wilson martèle depuis deux ans. Le polisario est, d’après ses mots répétés, une milice marxiste soutenue par l’Iran, le Hezbollah et la Russie, qui offre à Téhéran un avant-poste stratégique en Afrique. Le Royaume, lui, demeure à ses yeux un pilier de sécurité de l’Atlantique au Sahel et un allié des États-Unis depuis plus de deux siècles et demi. items.title: GES investigates alleged assault on student by two Techiman SHS teachers
items.description: The Ghana Education Service (GES) has launched an investigation into a video circulating on social media that appears to show two teachers of Techiman Senior High School (SHS) assaulting a student. In a press release issued on Saturday, October 31, 2026, the Service identified the teachers as Mr Jerry Jones Owusu Bekoe and Mr Adusa Ameyaw. The statement, signed by the Head of Public Relations, Daniel Fenyi, said the school’s disciplinary committee had held an initial hearing into the incident. “The committee’s findings are expected to be submitted to Management through the Regional Directorate in the coming days to inform further action and decisions,” the GES said. The GES identified the affected student as Seedorf Abeka Ampah, a final-year Agricultural Science student. It said he had received medical attention and was responding positively to treatment. “The affected student has received medical attention and is responding positively to treatment,” the statement added. The Service has appealed to the public to remain calm while investigations into the incident continue. It said the disciplinary committee’s findings would guide management’s next steps. The teachers’ culpability has not yet been established, and the GES is expected to determine any disciplinary measures after considering the committee’s findings.

items.title: Paris | La « Saison Méditerranée » s’achève sur une exposition dédiée au cinéma et au Maghreb
items.description: La cérémonie de clôture de la « Saison Méditerranée 2026 » a permis de dresser le bilan d'une édition riche de 500 manifestations et d'inaugurer l'exposition « Une Histoire du Cinéma Français : Héritages Maghrébins » au Palais de la Porte Dorée. L’ambassadeur de Tunisie en France, Dhia Khaled, a pris part à la cérémonie; présidée par Nadia Hai, déléguée interministérielle pour la Méditerranée et qui s'est déroulée en présence de la présidente de l’Institut français (chef de file de l'événement), ainsi que de représentants des ministères français de l’Europe et des Affaires étrangères et de la Culture, de diplomates et de figures du monde des arts. Cette manifestation d'envergure a débuté le 16 mai dernier et a proposé près de 500 spectacles et projets artistiques déployés en France, en Tunisie (avec 29 événements organisés à l'échelle nationale) et dans quatre autres pays de la rive sud. Ce programme ambitieux a mis en relief la vitalité créative et le pluralisme culturel du bassin méditerranéen, avec un accent particulier porté sur le patrimoine maghrébin. L'ambassade rappelle par ailleurs que la fin du festival marque l'inauguration de l’exposition « Une Histoire du Cinéma Français : Héritages Maghrébins », au Palais de la Porte Dorée à Paris et qui se poursuivra jusqu’au 21 mars 2027. items.title: La Société Nationale des Autoroutes du Maroc informe sur un accident sur l’autoroute Marrakech-Agadir
items.description: À la suite de l’accident survenu ce samedi 31 octobre 2026 à 00h57min au niveau du point kilométrique PK 411+720 de l’Autoroute Casablanca-Agadir, sens Casablanca vers Agadir, la Société Nationale des Autoroutes du Maroc (ADM) apporte les éclaircissements suivants : L’accident a impliqué un autocar, 2 véhicules légers et un poids lourd. Le poids lourd, après la crevaison d’un pneu, a entamé une manœuvre pour stationner sur la bande d’arrêt d’urgence (BAU), les deux véhicules légers qui le suivaient ont ralenti. L’autocar, qui circulait dans le même sens, est alors entré en collision avec 2 les véhicules légers. Dès la détection de l'incident, ADM, à travers son dispositif de supervision et de coordination, a immédiatement informé l'ensemble des intervenants : Gendarmerie Royale, Protection Civile, autorités locales et services de dépannage ; Les équipes d’ADM se sont mobilisées pour sécuriser le lieu de l’accident. Le bilan provisoire de l’accident fait état de 4 tués, 4 blessés graves et 28 blessés légers. Un deuxième accident a eu lieu à 100 mètres, dans le même sens de la circulation, impliquant 3 véhicules légers et 2 poids lourds, et occasionnant des dégâts matériels. Les deux accidents ont causé un ralentissement de la circulation dans le sens Casablanca vers Agadir L'ensemble des équipes est intervenu, chacune dans son périmètre de compétence, pour gérer la circulation, évacuer les victimes et dégager l’ensemble des véhicules impliqués. La circulation a été interrompue entre 02h40 à 03h10 afin de permettre l’intervention des engins de dépannage. A 04h04, une déviation du trafic vers l’échangeur d’Argana a été opérée afin de soulager la circulation. Les opérations d’intervention ont pris fin à 07h34. Les investigations se poursuivent sous la conduite des autorités compétentes afin de déterminer les causes de l’accident. ADM présente ses sincères condoléances aux familles des personnes décédées, et souhaite un prompt rétablissement aux blessés. ADM rappelle à ses clients-usagers l'importance de faire preuve de la plus grande vigilance, de respecter les limitations de vitesse et les distances de sécurité et d'éviter toute conduite en état de fatigue ou de somnolence. items.title: Gov’t to fund travel costs for mother of slain teenager to attend son’s funeral in New York
items.description: The Government of Ghana will cover the full travel costs of Madam Doris Adu Gyamfi, the mother of 15-year-old Javits Frimpong, to enable her to travel to New York to pay her final respects to her son. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced the decision in a post on X on Saturday, October 31, 2026, following the intervention of New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and US President Donald Trump in securing a visa for the bereaved mother. Mr Ablakwa welcomed the intervention, saying Ghana appreciated the efforts of the two leaders. “This is most appreciated, @NYCMayor. The Government of Ghana welcomes your intervention and President Trump’s timely decision. We have always known we can count on our own Kwame Mamdani,” he wrote. The Minister said he had spoken with Madam Gyamfi on Friday and assigned officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to assist her with the visa application process. He described her grief as unimaginable and said the government considered it important for her to be present to pay her last respects to her son. The Mahama administration, he added, would also contribute towards a dignified funeral for Javits. “We resolve to continue to work together in securing justice for Javits,” Mr Ablakwa stated. Javits, a 15-year-old Ghanaian student, was shot dead in the Bronx on Thursday, October 29, 2026, while on his way to school. He had moved from Ghana to the United States about a year earlier to join his father, Thomas Frimpong. His father has said he suspects the shooting may be linked to bullying his son allegedly experienced at school. Police have not publicly established a motive for the killing. The announcement of the government’s support follows Mayor Mamdani’s disclosure that President Trump had agreed, after a telephone conversation, to facilitate an immediate visa for Madam Gyamfi. The killing has drawn attention in Ghana and the United States, with calls for a thorough investigation and justice for the teenager. Madam Gyamfi is expected to travel to New York in the coming days. Investigations into the shooting are ongoing, and no arrests have been announced.

items.title: New York City Mayor Mamdani secures Trump’s approval for visa for mother of slain Ghanaian teenager in Bronx
items.description: The mother of 15-year-old Ghanaian student Javits Frimpong, who was fatally shot while walking to school in New York, will be granted a visa to travel to the United States following an intervention by President Donald Trump, New York City Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani has announced. Mr Mamdani disclosed the development in a post on X on Saturday, October 31, 2026, after a telephone conversation with President Trump. He said the arrangement would allow the bereaved mother, who is in Ghana, to travel to New York and say goodbye to her son in person. “The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away. Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately. All of New York City is mourning this tragedy,” he wrote. The mayor did not specify the type of visa to be issued or the arrangements for its processing. Javits was shot in the abdomen shortly before 9:30 a.m. on Thursday, October 29, while walking to school in the Claremont neighbourhood of the Bronx. The 15-year-old, a 10th-grade student at DreamYard Preparatory School, was taken to St. Barnabas Hospital by responding police officers but later died from his injuries. He had moved from Ghana to the United States in 2025 to live with his father, Thomas Frimpong, a yellow cab driver in New York. Mr Frimpong has expressed concern that bullying his son allegedly experienced at school may have been connected to the shooting. He said the school’s principal had previously informed him about an incident involving two students who had allegedly harassed Javits and were subsequently suspended. According to the father, his son had repeatedly complained about being bullied. He has appealed to those responsible for the shooting to surrender to the police. “I will tell them to give themselves to the police. I don’t think they are going to go free for killing an innocent child,” he said. However, police have not established a motive for the killing or confirmed any connection between the alleged bullying and the shooting. The Government of Ghana has condemned the killing and called on US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and ensure that those responsible are brought to justice. Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has spoken with the victim’s father to express the government’s condolences and assure the family of its support. Officials from Ghana’s Permanent Mission in New York have also visited the family. “We will pursue justice, and we will make sure that those who did this do not get away with it,” Mr Ablakwa said. Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Victor Emmanuel Smith, has also called for a thorough and impartial investigation, citing reports of bullying the teenager allegedly experienced at school. The New York Police Department is investigating the shooting and searching for up to three male suspects believed to be teenagers. Police have not publicly established their identities or a motive for the attack. No arrests had been announced as of Saturday, October 31. The killing has sparked grief among members of the Ghanaian community in New York and renewed calls for answers about the circumstances surrounding the teenager’s death. The visa arrangement announced by Mayor Mamdani is expected to enable Javits’ mother to travel from Ghana to be with her family and participate in the farewell arrangements.

items.title: Assemblée nationale : les députés adoptent le volet recettes de la LFR 2026, réévalué à 60 064 milliards GNF, en hausse de 7,53 %
items.description: Les députés de l’Assemblée nationale ont adopté, ce samedi 31 octobre 2026, en session extraordinaire, le volet recettes du projet de loi de finances rectificative (PLFR) 2026. Selon le rapport élaboré par la Commission des affaires économiques et financières, du Plan et de la Coopération, présenté par le rapporteur général, les recettes prévisionnelles du budget de l’État sont désormais fixées à 60 064,47 milliards de francs guinéens (GNF), contre 55 858,10 milliards dans la loi de finances initiale (LFI) 2026, soit une augmentation de 4 206,37 milliards GNF, correspondant à une progression de 7,53 %. Cette révision intervient dans un contexte marqué par les nouvelles orientations économiques et budgétaires du Gouvernement, notamment celles liées à la mise en œuvre du programme Simandou 2040, ainsi que par les évolutions de la conjoncture économique nationale et internationale. Dans son rapport, la commission parlementaire rappelle que la loi de finances rectificative constitue un instrument d’ajustement budgétaire permettant à l’État de tenir compte des nouvelles réalités économiques, financières et sociales intervenues après l’adoption du budget initial. Le Gouvernement avait transmis le projet de PLFR 2026 à l’Assemblée nationale le 17 octobre dernier, conformément aux dispositions de la Loi organique relative aux lois de finances (LORF). Sur le plan macroéconomique, les nouvelles prévisions font état d’un taux d’inflation révisé à 5,2 %, contre 3,5 % initialement prévu. L’objectif de croissance économique a, quant à lui, été revu à la baisse, passant de 9,5 % à 8,6 %. Le PIB nominal est également ramené de 401 670 milliards à 392 503 milliards GNF. En revanche, le taux de pression fiscale devrait atteindre 14,23 % du PIB, contre 12,13 % dans les prévisions initiales. Le déficit budgétaire connaît une légère amélioration, passant de 2,07 % à 2,01 % du PIB. Le rapport prend également en compte les pertes de recettes pétrolières consenties par l’État pour maintenir le prix du carburant à la pompe à 12 000 GNF, ainsi qu’une provision de 913 milliards GNF destinée à financer la subvention de stabilisation des prix des produits pétroliers. Des recettes fiscales en hausse de 8,39 % Dans le détail, les recettes du budget général sont réévaluées à 57 664,90 milliards GNF, contre 53 431,86 milliards dans la loi de finances initiale, soit une progression de 7,92 %. Les recettes fiscales représentent l’essentiel de cette augmentation. Elles sont désormais estimées à 52 795,68 milliards GNF, contre 48 709,96 milliards dans les prévisions initiales, soit une hausse de 4 085,72 milliards GNF (8,39 %). Cette progression s’explique principalement par l’augmentation des recettes issues des impôts sur les biens et services, qui enregistrent une hausse de 5 248,55 milliards GNF, soit 24,20 %, ainsi que celle des autres recettes fiscales, en progression de 785,79 milliards GNF (72,72 %). Toutefois, cette performance est atténuée par la baisse des recettes provenant des impôts sur le commerce extérieur et les transactions internationales (-1 340,59 milliards GNF), des impôts sur les revenus, les bénéfices et les gains en capital (-584,06 milliards GNF), ainsi que des impôts sur les salaires et la main-d’œuvre (-23,97 milliards GNF). Les prévisions de dons du budget général restent, pour leur part, inchangées à 1 952,40 milliards GNF. Quant aux autres recettes, elles sont réévaluées à 2 916,82 milliards GNF, contre 2 769,50 milliards dans la LFI 2026, soit une augmentation de 5,32 %. Les budgets d’affectation spéciale en légère baisse Contrairement au budget général, les recettes des Budgets d’affectation spéciale (BAS) connaissent une légère diminution. Elles sont estimées à 2 399,57 milliards GNF, contre 2 426,24 milliards initialement prévus, soit une baisse de 26,67 milliards GNF (-1,10 %). Cette évolution concerne notamment le Fonds national de développement local (FNDL), dont les recettes passent de 1 171,39 à 1 114,44 milliards GNF, soit une diminution de 4,86 %. Le Fonds d’investissement minier (FIM) enregistre également une baisse de 18,98 milliards GNF, ramenant ses recettes à 371,48 milliards. À l’inverse, le Fonds de développement des communes de Conakry (FODECCON) voit ses ressources augmenter de 49,26 milliards GNF, pour atteindre 698,63 milliards. Les recettes du Fonds commun de l’éducation (FCE) restent, quant à elles, maintenues à 215,02 milliards GNF. L’Assemblée nationale interpelle les régies financières et exige l’application des taxes sur les jeux de hasard Au-delà des projections budgétaires, la commission parlementaire a formulé plusieurs recommandations à l’endroit du Gouvernement et des administrations concernées. S’agissant de la mobilisation des recettes publiques, les députés invitent les régies financières à redoubler d’efforts pour élargir substantiellement l’assiette fiscale. Ils préconisent notamment l’identification de nouvelles sources de recettes, la formalisation progressive des entreprises du secteur informel, l’accélération de la digitalisation des procédures de déclaration, de liquidation et de recouvrement, ainsi que le renforcement des mécanismes de contrôle et d’évaluation du rendement fiscal. La question de l’application de la taxe sur les jeux de hasard a également retenu l’attention des parlementaires. Le rapport rappelle que deux prélèvements avaient été institués dans le cadre de l’examen du volet recettes de la loi de finances initiale 2025 : une taxe de 15 % sur le produit brut des jeux et un prélèvement de 7 % au titre du bénéfice non commercial (BNC) sur les gains supérieurs à un million de francs guinéens. Cependant, selon la commission, l’Autorité de régulation des jeux et pratiques assimilées (ARSJPA), à travers un courrier daté du 4 février 2025, aurait instruit les opérateurs du secteur de ne pas s’acquitter de ces taxes. Une situation que l’Assemblée nationale juge contraire au principe de la hiérarchie des normes et à l’obligation de respect des lois par les organes de l’État. En conséquence, les députés invitent la ministre en charge des Finances à prendre les dispositions nécessaires pour assurer l’application effective de ces mesures fiscales. Plus de 15 666 milliards GNF de dépenses fiscales dénoncés Autre préoccupation majeure soulevée dans le rapport : le coût des dépenses fiscales, notamment les exonérations et les régimes dérogatoires accordés dans le secteur minier et dans d’autres domaines de l’économie. Selon les données présentées à la commission, les dépenses fiscales douanières ont été évaluées à 11 793 milliards GNF en 2025, sur un montant de 24 500 milliards GNF de recettes douanières fiscales mobilisées, soit l’équivalent de 48 % des recettes collectées. Du côté de la Direction générale des impôts, les dépenses fiscales auraient atteint 3 873 milliards GNF pour les seuls neuf premiers mois de l’année 2026. Au total, le manque à gagner pour les finances publiques dépasserait ainsi 15 666 milliards GNF, soit environ 4 % du PIB, au titre des données présentées dans le rapport. La commission souligne également qu’un précédent rapport de la commission des Finances du Conseil national de la transition (CNT) avait révélé qu’en 2023, sur 128 mesures génératrices de dépenses fiscales, seulement dix, soit moins de 8 %, étaient à l’origine de 67 % des pertes définitives de recettes fiscales, évaluées à 2 329,2 milliards GNF. À travers ces observations, les députés attirent l’attention du Gouvernement sur la nécessité de mieux encadrer les exonérations fiscales et douanières, d’en évaluer régulièrement les retombées économiques et sociales et de renforcer les mécanismes de contrôle afin de limiter les pertes de recettes pour le budget national. L’adoption du volet recettes du PLFR 2026 marque ainsi une étape importante dans le processus d’ajustement des prévisions budgétaires de l’État. Elle met également en lumière les attentes du Parlement en matière de mobilisation des ressources internes, de discipline fiscale et de préservation des équilibres financiers, dans un contexte où le Gouvernement entend accélérer la mise en œuvre du programme Simandou 2040. items.title: We need to hold political actors in galamsey-affected areas accountable – Awula Serwah
items.description: The Executive Director of Eco-Conscious Citizens, Awula Serwah, has called for political actors in areas affected by illegal mining to be held accountable for the activities taking place in their jurisdictions. She said political authorities must take responsibility for the activities of illegal miners in their respective areas and ensure that all available resources are deployed to tackle the menace before it is too late. Speaking on JoyNews’ News File on Saturday, October 31, Ms Serwah said Ghana must move beyond repeated discussions on illegal mining and focus on enforcing existing laws to address the problem. “We know what to do, but we are pathologically allergic to enforcement,” she said. She stressed the need for stricter measures to curb illegal mining, including ending the indiscriminate issuance of mining licences and stopping the importation of excavators. “We have to stop issuing mining licences like confetti, stop the importation of excavators, and put all our resources into dealing with this cancer before it kills all of us,” she stated. Ms Serwah warned that the country was approaching an ecological catastrophe if urgent measures were not taken to address the activities of illegal miners. She called for a coordinated effort and stronger enforcement of mining regulations, insisting that the country must use every available resource to stop the menace before its environmental consequences become irreversible.

items.title: I’ve not seen any progress in the galamsey fight since Ex-President Kufuor’s tenure – Sulemana Braimah
items.description: Chief Executive Officer of the Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), Sulemana Braimah, says he has not observed any significant progress in Ghana’s fight against illegal mining, despite several interventions by successive governments. According to him, “To the point of whether this government is fighting galamsey, we are making progress or not, to be honest with you, I have not seen any progress,” he said. He argues that the country appears to be repeating measures that have been implemented by previous administrations without achieving lasting results in curbing the menace. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 31, Mr Braimah said interventions to tackle illegal mining could be traced back to the early 2000s, when former President John Agyekum Kufuor introduced Operation Flush Out. He said subsequent administrations, including those of the late President John Evans Atta Mills, John Dramani Mahama and Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, had each introduced measures to address the problem. “What is happening has happened before; it started under President Kufuor. President Kufuor set up Operation Flash Out and deployed the troops. After President Kufuor, President Atta Mills came in and continued what President Kufuor was doing.” “In 2014, President Mahama set up the Inter-Ministerial Committee to deal with the illegal mining thing; military men were deployed, and at some point, four hundred excavators were announced to be seized. All the way to President Akufo-Addo,” he added. According to him, the return of President John Mahama in 2025 has not, so far, convinced him that the country is making meaningful progress towards ending illegal mining. He maintained that while successive governments had taken various actions and announced interventions, these had not translated into the desired results. “If it is about actions that we can speak to, that they did that and did this….. so in terms of the fight, I believe if it is about what is happening with NAIMOS, forest reserves recovered is fine, but we still have our water bodies polluted, we still have galamseyers on the field,” he added.

items.title: Galamsey: Government’s progress claims not fully supported by figures – Prof Appiagyei-Tuah
items.description: An Associate Professor at the University of Ghana School of Law, Prof Kwadwo Appiagyei-Tuah, says that while some progress has been made in the fight against illegal mining, available data still point to an alarming situation. He cautioned against relying on government figures that have not been adequately substantiated, arguing that claims of progress must be backed by credible evidence. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile programme on Saturday, October 31, Prof. Appiagyei-Tuah said there was information suggesting that the government had made some gains in tackling galamsey, but questioned whether the figures being cited accurately reflected the situation on the ground. “Definitely some progress has been made, but there are some figures that have been thrown about without evidence,” he said. He maintained that although the government could point to some interventions and achievements, other available figures showed that illegal mining remained a serious national concern. The law lecturer’s comments come amid renewed debate over the effectiveness of government measures to combat galamsey, including arrests, equipment seizures, river protection operations and plans to reclaim degraded lands. President John Dramani Mahama has reported the confiscation of more than 8,200 items linked to illegal mining, including 135 excavators and nearly 200 firearms. He has also announced plans to reclaim 5,000 acres of degraded land from 2027, backed by GH¢200 million. Prof. Appiagyei-Tuah’s assessment adds to calls for greater transparency in reporting the results of the anti-galamsey campaign, with credible data needed to establish the extent of progress and the scale of the remaining environmental threat.

items.title: Gov’t going round in circles in the fight against galamsey – Erastus Asare Donkor
items.description: Investigative and environmental journalist Erastus Asare Donkor has accused the government of going round in circles in the fight against illegal mining, saying that its approach is largely similar to that of the previous Akufo-Addo administration. He says although the current government appears more willing to listen to concerns about illegal mining, its actions do not match its public pronouncements, raising questions about its commitment to ending the menace. Speaking on JoyNews ’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 31, during a discussion on the Mahama administration’s fight against galamsey, Mr Asare Donkor said the government’s approach suggested a lack of the urgency required to defeat illegal mining, stressing that a serious fight against the practice demanded the full commitment and resources of the state. “You’re tempted to say that we are moving around in circles. You see, if you are very interested in fighting something, you put all your arsenals into it,” he said. Mr Asare Donkor said the government was repeating strategies that had failed in the past while failing to provide the necessary resources to those tasked with tackling the problem. “I would say that basically we are doing the same thing, aside from the strategy that maybe NAIMOS may be adopting now, under the current leadership. That may be slightly different. But mostly, we are doing the same thing,” he said. He said that the previous Akufo-Addo administration handled the galamsey crisis with little regard for concerns raised by stakeholders, while the current government, despite being more receptive to such concerns, was not acting in line with its promises. “The previous administration treated this issue with kid gloves. They did not listen to anybody. The current administration, though they listen, they act differently, contrary to what they say,” he stated. Mr Asare Donkor called on President John Dramani Mahama to make Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) more accountable for illegal mining activities within their jurisdictions. He said that the district and municipal chief executives, who chair their respective security councils, were better placed to identify illegal mining operations in their communities because of their knowledge of the local terrain. He said relying heavily on NAIMOS without holding local authorities responsible would undermine the fight, as illegal miners could easily return to areas after task force personnel had left. “The DCEs, the MMDCEs, these are chairmen of districts and municipal security councils. They know every nook and cranny of the local area. If they are not being put to task to police their own areas, then we can send NAIMOS on a wild goose chase,” he said. He warned that without sustained monitoring and accountability, the gains made during enforcement operations would quickly be lost. “After they’ve left, the place will come back to zero, as we’ve been seeing it,” he added. Mr Asare Donkor insisted that the President must begin holding his own appointees responsible for what happens within their respective areas of authority. “Until the President starts holding his own appointees to account, hold them responsible for their own jurisdictions. If we don’t do that, then we are fighting a wild goose chase, and it will come to nothing,” he said.

items.title: ‘There’s no leadership in this galamsey fight’ – Prof Bokpin goes hard on President Mahama
items.description: Professor of Finance and Economist at the University of Ghana, Prof Godfred Bokpin, has criticised President John Mahama’s handling of illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey, saying the fight lacks the leadership needed to address the scale of the problem. He described the destruction caused by illegal mining as evil and questioned how those responsible could continue to damage the environment without facing decisive action from the State. Speaking on JoyNews ’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 31, during a discussion on the Mahama administration’s fight against galamsey, Prof Bokpin said the situation reflected a failure of leadership and accountability. “My considered view is that this is evil. This is evil. There’s nobody created in the image and likeness of God who would tolerate this. Nobody,” he said. To illustrate what he considers a lack of direction in the fight, the economist referred to Judges 21:25 in the Bible, which describes a period when there was no king in Israel, and people did whatever they considered right. Quoting the passage, he said: “In those days, there was no king in Israel, and everybody did what was right in his own eyes.” Prof Bokpin argued that the situation surrounding illegal mining in Ghana reflected a similar absence of leadership, with people acting without sufficient control or accountability. “In this galamsey business, there’s no leadership. Everybody is doing as they see fit in their own eyes,” he said. He further pointed to the constitutional responsibility of the President to protect the country’s natural resources, saying that the environment is held in trust for the people of Ghana. “It’s not for nothing the constitution puts all of these things under the care of the President to hold this in trust for the people of Ghana.” He questioned why the destruction was being allowed to continue despite the responsibility placed on the highest office of the land to safeguard the country’s natural heritage. “What are we doing to ourselves? We are becoming less and less human beings. How can we do this to ourselves? Who would we run to?” he asked. Prof Bokpin also mentioned what he described as attempts to place the blame for illegal mining on low-level operators while overlooking the influential individuals and interests behind the activities. He said that the scale of illegal mining could not be explained solely by the involvement of ordinary miners, particularly when heavy equipment and other resources were required. “Which JHS leaver can import a changfan?” he said, questioning the tendency to focus on lower-level operators rather than those financing and facilitating the activities. The economist said illegal mining had existed in Ghana for decades but had expanded to a more worrying scale as politically connected individuals and interests became involved. He said that the problem had moved beyond small-scale operators, with powerful interests allegedly investing in and benefiting from the illegal mining business. Turning to President Mahama, Prof Bokpin warned that the government could not claim to be managing the economy effectively while the environmental foundations on which economic activity depends continued to deteriorate. He said that environmental protection must be treated as an essential part of economic management. “Mr President, you cannot talk about managing an economy when the very foundation of this economy, being the environment, the ecological integrity, is being compromised,” he said. “I’m very sorry, Mr President. I’m very sorry.”

items.title: Mahama gov’t repeating Akufo-Addo-era mistakes in galamsey fight – Erastus Asare Donkor
items.description: Investigative and Environmental Journalist at the Multimedia Group Limited, Erastus Asare Donkor, says the John Mahama administration is repeating many of the approaches used by the previous Akufo-Addo government in the fight against illegal mining, popularly known as galamsey. According to him, the government’s response has not been sufficiently different or forceful to match the scale of environmental destruction, despite some progress made by the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS). Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 31, during a discussion on the Mahama administration’s fight against galamsey, Mr Asare Donkor said the country appeared to be repeating past mistakes rather than adopting a more effective strategy. Asked how the current government’s approach compared with the initial stages of the eight-year Akufo-Addo administration, he said, “Basically, we are doing the same thing, aside from the strategy that maybe NAIMOS may be adopting now under the current leadership. That may be slightly different.” He said that although the previous administration failed to give the problem the attention it deserved, the current government was also not matching its public statements with action. “The previous administration treated this issue with kid gloves. They did not listen to anybody. The current administration, though they listen, they act differently, contrary to what they say,” he stated. Mr Asare Donkor said a government genuinely committed to ending illegal mining must deploy all the resources available to it, including personnel, equipment, logistics and funding. Using the military analogy, he explained that defeating an enemy required a well-resourced strategy informed by a proper understanding of the threat. “In the military, if you want to defeat an enemy, you put all your arsenals, you bring in the weapons, you study the enemy, and you bring out everything that you have to deal with it. We are not seeing that,” he said. He complained that personnel assigned to combat illegal mining often lacked the basic resources needed to operate effectively. According to him, the officers require pick-up vehicles, equipment, canoes, and logistics to reach affected communities, as well as money to fuel vehicles and support personnel deployed in remote areas. He alleged that the officers sometimes had to plead for resources, only to receive small amounts that were eventually exhausted. “They need money to fuel vehicles, to pay soldiers in the bushes. And sometimes they have to go and beg, and then a little part of the resources are released to them, just as it has been released now. And then after some time, it goes away,” he said. “We are not doing much as we are talking about. The seriousness is not being seen,” he added. When asked why he continued to visit illegal mining sites despite the risks involved, Mr Asare Donkor said he considered documenting environmental destruction a responsibility to future generations. “It’s my duty. I feel that I have to do this for generations unborn. At least that’s my job, to document it. So, I’ll do it,” he said. He noted that investigative reporting helped to draw attention to the destruction of several forest reserves and said sustained media coverage had contributed to efforts to protect some of them. He cited the Tano Anwia and Tano Nimri forest areas, as well as Yor Yor, Boi River and the Jimera Extension, as places where consistent reporting had helped keep illegal mining activities in the public eye. “If we had not done the consistent reporting on Tano Anwia, that forest would have been gone by now,” he said. He also welcomed efforts by the Ghana Gold Board to reclaim 50 hectares of the affected forest, although he noted that a significant portion of the 192 hectares destroyed remained to be recovered. Mr Asare Donkor further disclosed that more than 150 excavators had been seized from illegal mining areas, including Tano Anwia, Tano Nimri, Yor Yor and Boi River, with some currently parked at Samreboi. He described these developments as important gains in the fight but warned that new methods of illegal mining were threatening progress made in protecting forest reserves.

items.title: Honesty, patriotism key to ending galamsey – Sulemana Braimah
items.description: Chief Executive Officer of the Media Foundation for West Africa (MFWA), Sulemana Braimah, says ending illegal mining in Ghana will require honesty and a strong sense of patriotism from the country’s two major political parties. He believes the governing National Democratic Congress (NDC) and the opposition New Patriotic Party (NPP) must demonstrate genuine commitment to the fight rather than allow partisan interests to undermine efforts to address the menace. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, October 31, Mr Braimah said both parties were aware that some of their members were involved in illegal mining but continued to politicise the issue. He argued that the two parties also understood that ending galamsey would not be easy, given the interests and networks sustaining the practice. He said only a commitment to honesty and patriotism, with both parties willing to put the national interest above political considerations, could help bring an end to illegal mining. “What it takes [To end galamsey], for me at this stage, is honesty and a sense of patriotism. If the NDC today would want to tell Ghanaians that we knew what the problem was, we knew the fight was going to be difficult, but maybe we did politics with it to come to power, maybe we will all understand. The NPP can also acknowledge so that, together as a country, we confront what our common enemy is,” he said. He therefore called on the NDC and NPP to demonstrate sincerity and take collective responsibility for tackling the menace.
